A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same shrinkage-baseline research. All 27 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical and logic-reasoning experiments, five-seed GSM8k comparisons, and baseline-error and gradient-variance measurements in Section 4 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Geometry3k, RLHF, direct gradient-error measurements, and heterogeneity studies in Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendices B–C.

M1.justification: The two-level leave-one-out means, estimated shrinkage coefficient, and resulting advantage calculation remain unchanged. v1 Equations 8–14 match v2 Equations 10–16, and Listing 1 is functionally equivalent. The added applications use the existing method.

E1.justification: v2 adds image-based Geometry3k reasoning and a six-dataset RLHF mixture evaluated on Arena-Hard-v0.1/v2.0 and Arena-Creative-Writing. Appendix C introduces mixed-difficulty and mixed-task scenarios, including KnK-9. Qwen2.5 math training is now reported as DAPO17k alone, replacing the stated DAPO17k-plus-MATH12k coverage.

E2.justification: The value-function MSE comparison changes from JS, RLOO, and BLOO in v1 Figure 6 to JS, RLOO, REINFORCE++, and ReMax in v2 Figure 9. The six-method GSM8k comparison remains intact. The new RLHF table also includes the original Llama model as a control.

E3.justification: The value-function reference estimate changes from 32 to 128 trajectories per question. New protocols include gradient-error estimation using 128 questions with 256 responses each, controlled heterogeneity experiments, multimodal training, and reward-model-based RLHF with win-rate evaluation. These are documented protocol additions or revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's baseline-MSE and training-dynamics analyses, v2 adds direct gradient-error comparisons against a Monte Carlo reference in Appendix B.2. Appendix C tests difficulty heterogeneity through KnK mixtures and semantic heterogeneity through matched-pass-rate KnK/Countdown mixtures and shrinkage-coefficient sweeps, directly examining when cross-prompt pooling helps.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.1 explicitly states that random seeds are fixed for the mathematical-reasoning comparisons; v2 omits this assurance. GSM8k retains the same five named seeds and individual-run results. No new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds multimodal, RLHF, gradient-error, and heterogeneity results. Table 1 reports JS RLHF win rates of 56.7/7.4/23.4%, versus RLOO's 55.3/5.6/20.2%. Figure 4 revises the Countdown curves, while Figure 3 removes Qwen3's AMC23 results. The GSM8k and KnK subset tables retain their numerical values.

T1.justification: The core propositions, theorem, and proofs are retained after relocation. Limited mathematical changes include the displayed GRPO variance denominator changing from m−1 to m and an explicit Gaussian James–Stein estimator definition in v2 Section 5.3. Neither changes the proposed shrinkage formula.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims of a hyperparameter-free, unbiased, variance-reducing baseline remain substantially unchanged. v2's conclusion adds an explicit claim of applicability regardless of task difficulty or semantic heterogeneity, extending the stated generality of the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops new applicability interpretations: difficulty heterogeneity reduces selected shrinkage, while semantic mixing reduces the benefit without shifting the tested optimum. It also interprets RLHF results as extending applicability beyond binary verifiable rewards. Sections 3.2 and 5.3 explicitly distinguish the proposed rule from classical Gaussian James–Stein guarantees, which do not directly apply.

D1.justification: v2 adds multimodal hyperparameter/hardware configurations and identifies the RLHF reward model and training recipe. Existing implementation listings are retained, but micro-batch sizes disappear from the configuration tables. Qwen3 clipping becomes internally inconsistent: Section 4.1 specifies 0.25, while Appendix D.5 retains v1's 0.28.

R1.justification: v2 expands the statistical positioning with empirical-Bayes, minimax, and admissibility literature, including Efron–Morris, Baranchik, Brown, and Berger, while explicitly distinguishing its estimator from classical James–Stein shrinkage. It also adds discussion of small-rollout LLM practice, newer RLVR methods such as GSPO, and multimodal/RLHF research supporting the expanded scope.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially condensed and rewritten, with terminology shifting toward 'shrinkage baseline.' Proofs move from Appendix B to A, the main-text MSE analysis moves to Appendix B, and experimental material is reorganized into Appendix D's implementation, results, task-description, and settings sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn, numerous plots are recolored and rearranged, new experimental displays are added, and configuration tables use compact paired columns. The individual GSM8k-run plot is removed while its tabulated values remain, and the Qwen3 AMC23 panel disappears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the central mechanism: Appendix B.2 directly measures gradient error, and Appendix C investigates previously untested dependence on difficulty and semantic heterogeneity. Multimodal and learned-reward RLHF experiments test meaningful applicability boundaries, while the Gaussian James–Stein qualification clarifies theoretical scope. These gains outweigh limited reporting regressions, particularly omitted micro-batch sizes and conflicting Qwen3 clipping values; the core theoretical proofs remain unchanged.
